subject: biology
title: Digestive enzymes
key_idea: Carbohydrases, proteases and lipases break food down into small soluble molecules. Bile helps lipase by neutralising stomach acid and emulsifying fat. The small molecules are used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.

sections.heading: The three types of digestive enzyme

blocks.text: Digestive enzymes convert food into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood. Each type acts on one type of food.
Carbohydrases break down carbohydrates to simple sugars. Amylase is the carbohydrase that breaks down starch.

diagram.alt: Sort each statement into amylase, protease or lipase.

items: Amylase: starch to sugars. Protease: protein to amino acids. Lipase: fat to fatty acids and glycerol.
The pancreas and small intestine make all three types.
Each product is small and soluble, so it can be absorbed.

blocks.text: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It is released into the small intestine, where it helps lipase.

items.meaning: Breaking large droplets of fat into many small droplets.

items: Bile is alkaline. It neutralises the hydrochloric acid that comes from the stomach.
This gives the correct pH for the enzymes in the small intestine.
Bile emulsifies fat. This gives small droplets with a larger surface area.
The alkaline conditions and the large surface area increase the rate of fat breakdown by lipase.

diagram.alt: How bile helps fat digestion: bile is released into the small intestine, neutralises acid, emulsifies fat into small droplets, giving a larger surface area, so lipase breaks the fat down faster.
steps: Bile released into the small intestine
Acid neutralised: correct pH for lipase

items: Bile is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder and is alkaline.
It emulsifies fat, which increases the surface area for lipase.
Bile does not digest fat. Lipase does.

blocks.text: The small molecules from digestion are absorbed into the blood. The body uses them to build new molecules, and some are used in respiration.

rows: Carbohydrates, such as starch and cellulose

items.meaning: A small molecule that joins with many others to make a polymer, for example an amino acid.
A large molecule made of many monomers joined together, for example a protein.

items: Some glucose is used in respiration.
Amino acids are joined to make the proteins the body needs for growth, such as muscle.
When lipase breaks down fat in milk, fatty acids are produced.
Fatty acids are acidic, so the pH of the mixture falls.
An indicator that is pink in alkaline conditions turns colourless as the pH falls.
Digestion products are used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.
Starch is made of sugar monomers. Proteins are made of amino acids.
Some glucose is used in respiration.

checks.q: Which organs in the human digestive system produce amylase?
checks.a: The salivary glands, the pancreas and the small intestine.

checks.q: How does bile help in the digestion of fats?
checks.a: It emulsifies fat, which increases the surface area of fat, so lipase can break it down faster. It also neutralises the acid from the stomach.

checks.q: Name the molecules produced when proteins and lipids are digested.
checks.a: Proteins give amino acids. Lipids give fatty acids and glycerol.

worked_example.question:
A person has a tumour blocking the tube leading from the gall bladder to the small intestine.

Explain why this person would have difficulty digesting fat.
answer_points: No or less bile reaches the small intestine.
So there is less or no emulsification of fat.
So there is a smaller surface area for lipase to break down the fat.
The pH of the small intestine is not neutralised, so it is acid or low.
So lipase is not at its optimum pH to break down fat.
worked_example.tip: Five separate marks. Link the effect of bile on the surface area and the effect on the pH.

worked_example.question:
5 cm³ of milk B and 1 cm³ of lipase were added to a test tube.

The pH of this mixture was pH 7.

This test tube was placed in a water bath for 10 minutes.

The pH of the mixture changed from pH 7 to pH 5.

Explain what caused this change in pH.
answer_points: Lipase digests fat (lipid). Breakdown is accepted for digest.
Forming fatty acids (and glycerol).
Which are acidic, lowering the pH of the mixture, or making the mixture more acidic.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each link in the chain: lipase, fatty acids, lower pH.

worked_example.question:
The cell wall in the plant cell is made from a carbohydrate called cellulose. Cellulose is a polymer.

Explain why sugars are needed to make the cell wall.
answer_points: Sugars are the monomers.
Sugars are joined together to make the polymer, cellulose.
Also allowed: sugar or glucose is the smallest unit of carbohydrate; cellulose is made up of glucose molecules.
worked_example.tip: Use the words monomer and polymer. Saying that cellulose is a polymer made up of sugar monomers scores both marks.

worked_example.question:
Starch and sucrose are made by plants after photosynthesis.
Describe how starch is broken down in the human digestive system so that it can be absorbed into the blood.
answer_points: Physical digestion uses the teeth in the mouth, and churning in the stomach.
Physical digestion increases the surface area for faster enzyme activity.
Chemical digestion breaks insoluble molecules down into smaller soluble molecules, using enzymes.
The salivary glands and pancreas make amylase.
Amylase breaks starch down to maltose.
Maltase is found on the lining (epithelium) of the small intestine.
Maltase breaks maltose down to glucose.
The optimum pH for amylase and maltase is neutral, about 7 to 8.
worked_example.tip: Any six of these points score the marks.

blocks.text: (Supplement) Starch and protein are each digested by more than one enzyme.

items.text: Amylase breaks starch down into the sugar maltose.
Maltase breaks maltose down into glucose. It works on the membranes of the cells lining the small intestine.

items: **Pepsin** is a protease made in the stomach. It breaks protein down in acidic conditions.
**Trypsin** is a protease made in the pancreas. It works in the small intestine in alkaline conditions.
Bile makes the contents of the small intestine alkaline, so trypsin can work.

blocks.text: Where enzymes are made and where they act

items: Amylase is made in the salivary glands, pancreas and small intestine. It acts in the mouth and the small intestine.
Protease is made in the stomach, pancreas and small intestine. It acts in the stomach and the small intestine.
Lipase is made in the pancreas and small intestine. It acts in the small intestine.
Chewing by the teeth and churning by the stomach break food into smaller pieces.
This increases the surface area of the food for enzymes to act on in chemical digestion.
They contain enzymes, such as protease and lipase, that break down protein and fat stains into soluble substances.
They work well at moderate temperatures. They stop working at high temperatures, because the enzymes are denatured.

worked_example.question: Describe how protein is digested in the human alimentary canal.
answer_points: A protease (peptidase) is involved.
Pepsin works in the stomach.
Digestion takes place in the small intestine (duodenum) or stomach, with protease released by the pancreas or stomach.
This produces amino acids (or dipeptides).
Trypsin from the pancreas, working in the duodenum, is also accepted.
worked_example.tip: Any three of these points score the marks.

blocks.text: Starch is digested in two steps, by two enzymes.

items.text: Amylase breaks starch down into the sugar maltose.
Maltase breaks maltose down into glucose. It is found on the lining of the small intestine.

items: Starch and glycogen are made of many simple sugar (glucose) units.
Protein is made of amino acids.
A lipid is made of three fatty acids joined to one glycerol.
